name: Hazor
title: Canaanite capital and the most powerful city-state of northern Canaan
summary: Hazor was the dominant power center of northern Canaan and the largest Canaanite city-state, described as "the head of all these kingdoms" (Josh 11:10). During the Israelite conquest, King Jabin of Hazor assembled a broad coalition of northern kings against Joshua, but was decisively defeated at the waters of Merom. Joshua then captured and burned the city—the only one of the high cities to be reduced to ashes. In the period of the judges, Hazor reemerged as a power when a new King Jabin, with his commander Sisera, oppressed Israel for twenty years until Deborah and Barak, through the Lord's intervention, shattered his military dominance. The city later regained strategic importance when King Solomon fortified it along with Megiddo and Gezer as part of the kingdom's defensive line. Hazor's history illustrates how God repeatedly intervened to break Canaanite supremacy and fulfill the promise of the land.

keyEvents.title: Jabin of Hazor leads the coalition against Israel
keyEvents.description: King Jabin of Hazor, who was the head of the northern Canaanite kingdoms, gathered a large coalition of kings at the waters of Merom to fight against the Israelites under Joshua's leadership.

keyEvents.title: Joshua defeats the coalition at the waters of Merom
keyEvents.description: Joshua launched a surprise attack on the Canaanite coalition at the Waters of Merom and defeated them with a great victory, just as the Lord had promised.

keyEvents.title: Joshua Burns Hazor
keyEvents.description: Joshua captured Hazor, struck down its king with the sword, and burned the city. The text emphasizes that Hazor had been the capital of all these kingdoms and was the only royal city Joshua burned.

keyEvents.title: Jabin of Hazor Oppresses Israel During the Period of the Judges
keyEvents.description: A new King Jabin of Hazor oppressed the Israelites for twenty years under his powerful commander Sisera. Deborah and Barak were raised up by the Lord to confront this threat.

keyEvents.title: Deborah and Barak Defeat Sisera
keyEvents.description: Through God's intervention, Barak and Deborah defeated Sisera's army at the Kishon River, and Jabin's dominion over Israel was gradually broken completely.

keyEvents.title: Solomon Fortifies Hazor
keyEvents.description: King Solomon rebuilt Hazor as one of his strategically fortified cities, along with Megiddo and Gezer, as part of the kingdom's major defense project.

versions.summary: Hazor was an important Canaanite city-state in northern Canaan. The city is best known as the place where King Jabin ruled and which was conquered and burned by Joshua during the conquest of the Promised Land. Later, the city reappears during the period of the Judges under another King Jabin.
versions.title: Canaanite Kingdom
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Canaanite Kingdom' is clear, but could be refined to reflect that Hazor was the most important and largest Canaanite city in the region, often described as 'the head of all these kingdoms' (Josh 11:10).; [critical] Hazor is a city/place, not a person. The role 'leader' is misleading. For a city-state profile, the roles should reflect what the place was: a Canaanite city-state, fortified city and strategic center.; [minor] The summary is good, but should also mention Solomon's rebuilding of the city as a fortress (1 Kings 9:15), since this is an important part of the city's biblical history.; [minor] The events cover the key occurrences well, including the conquest under Joshua, the period of the judges and Solomon's fortification. All scripture references appear correct (Josh=6, Judg=7, 1 Kgs=11).; [major] Footnotes are missing. Hazor is one of the most archaeologically excavated sites in Israel, with important findings by Yigael Yadin and others that confirm biblical accounts. This should be covered.

footnotes.text: Hazor (Hebrew: חָצוֹר, Ḥāṣôr) is identified with Tell el-Qedah (Tel Hazor) in Upper Galilee, about 14 km north of the Sea of Galilee. The name may mean 'enclosure' or 'settlement', possibly from the root ח-צ-ר meaning to surround or enclose.

Archaeological excavations at Tel Hazor, particularly led by Yigael Yadin (1955–1969) and later by Amnon Ben-Tor (from 1990), have uncovered a massive destruction layer from the 13th century BC that many scholars associate with Joshua's conquest. At its height, the city covered about 80 hectares and was the largest city in southern Levant during the Bronze Age.

In the Amarna letters (c. 1350 BC), Hazor is mentioned repeatedly, and the king of Hazor is described as a powerful ruler. Egyptian execration texts from the 18th and 19th dynasties also mention the city, confirming its prominent position in the region long before the Israelite conquest.

Joshua 11:10 refers to Hazor as 'the head of all these kingdoms,' indicating that the city served as a leading power center or dominant city-state within a coalition of Canaanite cities in northern Canaan.

Solomon's fortification of Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer (1 Kings 9:15) has been confirmed archaeologically through the discovery of similar six-chambered gates at all three sites, although the dating and attribution of these gates remain debated among scholars.

The appearance of a 'King Jabin of Hazor' in both Joshua 11 and Judges 4 has led to discussion among scholars. Some suggest that 'Jabin' may have been a dynastic title rather than a personal name, similar to the use of 'Pharaoh' in Egypt or 'Abimelech' among the Philistines.

In the Mari texts from the 18th century BC, Hazor is mentioned as an important trading center with connections to Babylon. This shows that the city's peak and influence extended far back in time and well beyond local Canaan.
